prompt.context: Our client, Shermer Pharma, is a venture-backed start-up pharmaceutical company. Over the past 15 years, Shermer has been developing a molecule that has been approved by the FDA to cure Alzheimer's with 90% efficacy. Shermer has no existing Sales or Marketing organization — the company has purely been a research firm to this point. FDA approval has been granted. The product is a pill that cures Alzheimer's, an illness that currently has no treatment that cures or stops the progress of the disease. Alzheimer's is a degenerative, terminal disease that causes senility and dementia. 30 million people suffer worldwide. Sales would be focused on Neurologists and Geriatric psychiatrists, not the consumer of the product. Shermer will be the only firm with a cure for the next 5 years.
prompt.question: Shermer's owners have hired us to answer two questions: (1) How should we sell our product? (2) Is our product going to be profitable?

clarifying_info.q: How many people suffer from Alzheimer's?
clarifying_info.a: 30 million people worldwide suffer from Alzheimer's.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the target customers / sales targets?
clarifying_info.a: Sales would be focused on Neurologists and Geriatric psychiatrists, not the end consumer.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have a sales or marketing organization?
clarifying_info.a: No. Shermer has no Sales or Marketing organization; it has purely been a research firm.
We will not focus on competitive response during this case — Shermer is the only firm with a cure for Alzheimer's and will be for the next 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: Has the FDA approved the product?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, FDA approval has been granted.

clarifying_info.q: What is the US market size for Alzheimer's?
clarifying_info.a: 5 million patients in the US (provide this number at the end of the sizing exercise).

exhibits.title: Sales Force Options
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of two sales force options: Develop Own Sales Force vs. Contract Sales Force. Rows include: Percent of visit focused on our product, Fully loaded annual cost of 1 sales rep, Cost per sales call, Total calls required, Total Sales Reps needed, and Total annual Selling Cost. Some cells are pre-filled and others are blank for the candidate to calculate.

exhibits.title: Annual Net Income
exhibits.shows: A five-year P&L table with rows for Projected Market Penetration, Total Users, Total Gross Margin, Amortized R&D Costs, Selling Costs, G&A Costs, and Net Income. Market penetration percentages are pre-filled; all other rows are blank for the candidate to calculate.

framework: Part 1 — Sales channel: Identify and compare options for building a Sales and Marketing function: (a) develop an internal own sales force, (b) use a contract sales organization, (c) sell Shermer to a larger pharma firm with existing capabilities.

Part 2 — Profitability: Size the addressable US Alzheimer's market, determine market penetration by year, calculate gross margin, subtract amortized R&D costs, selling costs, and G&A to arrive at net income over 5 years.
Synthesize: Determine which sales channel is financially optimal, whether the product reaches profitability within 5 years, and deliver a clear recommendation.

questions.prompt: What are the options for selling the product, and which is financially better?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify three options: (1) develop an own internal sales force, (2) use a contract sales organization, (3) sell Shermer to a larger firm. They should ask questions about sales force costs and structure to earn Exhibit 1. Using Exhibit 1, they should calculate the missing cells and compare total annual selling costs. Contract sales ($12MM/year) is cheaper than own sales force ($17MM/year). A strong candidate will also note that contract sales reps split their attention (50% on Shermer's product vs. 100% for own reps) — so for ~$5MM/year more, an own sales force may be more effective. Selling the company is qualitatively valid but has no supporting data.

math.setup: Exhibit 1 contains partially filled data. Calculate missing cells for both options. Own Sales Force: cost per call = ($200k × 85) / 100k calls = $170. Total annual cost = $200k × 85 = $17MM. Contract Sales Force: reps spend 50% on Shermer so total calls required = 100k / 50% = 200k. Total reps = 85 × 2 = 170. Total annual cost = $60 × 200k = $12MM.
steps: Own force cost per sales call: ($200k × 85) / 100k = $170 per call
Own force total calls required: 100,000 (given if asked)
Own force total annual selling cost: $200k × 85 reps = $17MM
Contract force total calls required: 100k / 50% = 200,000 calls
Contract force total reps needed: 85 × 2 = 170 reps
Contract force total annual selling cost: $60 × 200k = $12MM
math.answer: Contract sales force annual cost = $12MM; Own sales force = $17MM. Contract sales is $5MM/year cheaper.

questions.guidance: The candidate should attempt a market sizing. Interviewer provides the answer of 5MM US patients at the end of the sizing exercise regardless of candidate estimate. Ignore NPV; use straight-line amortization for R&D.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the 5-year P&L and determine whether the product is profitable.
questions.guidance: Candidate must ask for or derive key inputs: total market (5MM), annual gross margin per user ($1,000), R&D cost ($1.5B amortized straight-line over 5 years = $300MM/year), selling costs from Exhibit 1 ($12MM/year using contract sales), G&A costs ($25MM/year). Manufacturing and Packaging costs are included in Gross Margin. Tax can be ignored. Net income is negative in Year 1 but turns positive in Year 2. A strong candidate notes that taxes would not prevent hitting profit targets by Year 5.

math.setup: Total market = 5MM patients. Gross margin per user per year = $1,000. R&D = $1.5B / 5 = $300MM/year amortized. Selling costs = $12MM/year (contract). G&A = $25MM/year. Net Income = Gross Margin − Amortized R&D − Selling Costs − G&A.
steps: Year 1: Users = 5% × 5M = 250k; Gross Margin = 250k × $1k = $250MM; Net Income = $250MM − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM = −$87MM
Year 2: Users = 10% × 5M = 500k; Gross Margin = $500MM; Net Income = $500MM − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM = $163MM
Year 3: Users = 25% × 5M = 1.25MM; Gross Margin = $1.25B; Net Income = $1.25B − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM = $913MM
Year 4: Users = 40% × 5M = 2MM; Gross Margin = $2B; Net Income = $2B − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM = $1.663B
Year 5: Users = 60% × 5M = 3MM; Gross Margin = $3B; Net Income = $3B − $300MM − $12MM − $25MM = $2.663B
math.answer: Net Income: Year 1 = −$87MM, Year 2 = +$163MM, Year 3 = +$913MM, Year 4 = +$1.663B, Year 5 = +$2.663B. Product is profitable from Year 2; R&D fully recovered within 5 years.

brainstorming.prompt: What else should we consider before engaging this plan? (High-level strategic considerations)

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: $1,000/year for a life-saving cure appears significantly underpriced
Could price higher given no competition for 5 years and strong willingness to pay
Insurance reimbursement dynamics could affect accessible market size

categories.name: Sales Force Effectiveness
ideas: Contract sales reps split attention at 50% — may be less effective than own reps
$5MM/year incremental cost for own sales force may be justified given $3B revenue potential
Incentive alignment differs between own and contracted reps

categories.name: Strategic Alternatives
ideas: Sell Shermer to a large pharma firm with existing Sales and Marketing infrastructure
Partnership or licensing deal with established pharma could monetize the asset without building S&M
Evaluate acquisition offers vs. standalone profitability trajectory

categories.name: Market and Patient Access
ideas: Patient diagnosis rates — are all 5MM diagnosed and under specialist care?
Insurance and payer coverage — will insurers reimburse?

recommendation: Shermer Pharma should use a contract sales force to bring its Alzheimer's cure to market — this is the most financially efficient option at $12MM/year vs. $17MM/year for an own sales force, and Shermer has no existing Sales and Marketing capabilities.
The product will be profitable: it turns net-income-positive in Year 2 and generates $2.663B net income in Year 5, fully recovering the $1.5B R&D investment within the 5-year window.
Alternatively, Shermer should evaluate selling the company to a large pharma firm, which would avoid building any commercial infrastructure and could yield immediate value for owners.
risks: Contract reps focus only 50% of visits on Shermer's product, potentially limiting market penetration vs. projections
Year 1 net income is negative (−$87MM), requiring sufficient capital reserves
Pricing at $1,000/year appears well below market potential, leaving significant value on the table
No marketing capabilities — brand building and physician education will be challenging regardless of sales channel
next_steps: Assess strategic buyer interest and potential acquisition valuation
If proceeding independently, issue RFP to contract sales organizations and evaluate terms
Model sensitivity of profitability to higher price points
Develop physician education and awareness plan for product launch
